title: Section final: how Burst makes code fast
sub: Vectorization, data layout, determinism, debugging, polymorphism, transforms and physics — and when you need none of it
cards/0/body:
No new theory here — just what the questions will need.

  • Vectorization. Burst turns a tight loop into SIMD: one instruction for several floats at once. Branches get in the way (replace if with math.select), and so does aliasing (job containers are [NoAlias] by default). You check it in the Burst Inspector: packed mulps/vmulps instead of scalar mulss.
  • SoA vs AoS. Memory is read in cache lines. With AoS the line also carries fields the loop never touches; with SoA it holds only the values you need, back to back. That is why Entities stores components in chunks by type.
  • Determinism. FloatMode: Default = Strict; Fast reorders operations and may use FMA; Deterministic — since Burst 1.8.25, only on 64-bit architectures and only for Burst code. FloatPrecision sets the accuracy of math functions. Lockstep across platforms often uses fixed-point.
  • Debugging. Jobs > Burst > Enable Compilation turns Burst off so the ordinary debugger works; Enable Safety Checks controls the checks inside Burst code; Native Debug Mode Compilation or [BurstCompile(Debug = true)] is for a native debugger. Debug.Log in Burst takes a literal or $"..." with primitives and Mathematics vectors; a struct’s ToString() does not work.
  • Polymorphism and statics. A generic job with a struct rule when the type is known at compile time; FunctionPointer<T> when it is chosen at runtime, in batches; SharedStatic<T> for shared mutable statics, written atomically.
  • Engine objects. TransformAccessArray + IJobParallelForTransform (only different roots run in parallel), RaycastCommand and the other query batches.
  • When you don’t need it. Small data, branchy logic, managed dependencies. Profiler in a build first.
cards/1/q: In the Burst Inspector, the ClampJob loop is made of scalar mulss, and LLVM IR Optimization Diagnostics points at the branch in the body. What do you do first?
cards/1/options/0: Remove the branch: r[i] = math.select(0f, v[i] * k, v[i] > 0f), and check in the Inspector that the multiplies are now packed
cards/1/explain: math.select computes both values and picks one without a jump — every element takes the same path, and the loop can become SIMD. After the change, look in the Inspector for mulps or vmulps instead of mulss.
cards/1/wrong/1: Native containers in job fields are already treated as [NoAlias]; the branch is the problem.
cards/1/wrong/2: batchSize affects how iterations are handed to threads, not the instructions inside the loop.
cards/1/wrong/3: Deterministic is about identical results across platforms, not about vectorization.
cards/2/q: Explain out loud why SoA is faster than AoS. Put the steps of the answer in order.
cards/2/items/0: The CPU reads memory not byte by byte but in cache lines, usually 64 bytes
cards/2/items/1: With AoS the line carries the whole struct, including fields the loop never touches
cards/2/items/2: With SoA the line holds only the values the loop reads, back to back
cards/2/items/3: Burst loads contiguous values with one SIMD instruction — the loop vectorizes
cards/2/explain: Mechanism (cache lines) → what AoS wastes → what SoA gains → why it also means vectorization. That is the order to say it in an interview, finishing with: “and I check it in the Burst Inspector”.
cards/3/q: What is true about float determinism in Burst? Select all that apply.
cards/3/options/0: FloatMode.Deterministic is supported since Burst 1.8.25 and only on 64-bit architectures
cards/3/options/1: FloatMode.Fast may reorder operations and use FMA, so the result can differ from Strict
cards/3/options/2: FloatPrecision.High guarantees identical results on every platform
cards/3/options/3: FloatMode.Deterministic also makes the ordinary C# code around the job deterministic
cards/3/options/4: Lockstep across different platforms often uses fixed-point instead of float
cards/3/explain: Deterministic arrived in 1.8.25 and works only on 64-bit architectures and only for Burst code: non-deterministic inputs from outside break it. Fast trades accuracy for speed. FloatPrecision is about the accuracy of functions like sin and exp, not about matching across platforms.
cards/4/q: Interviewer: “A job gives wrong results with Burst and correct ones with Burst off. How do you track it down?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/4/options/0: I make sure Jobs > Burst > Enable Safety Checks is on, so Burst code catches out-of-bounds access. I look at FloatMode: Fast reorders operations. Then Debug.Log with primitives inside the Burst code, or [BurstCompile(Debug = true)] and a native debugger
cards/4/options/1: I call Debug.Log(ToString()) on the job struct inside Execute and compare the output
cards/4/options/2: Burst cannot be debugged, so I rewrite the job without Burst
cards/4/options/3: I set a breakpoint in Execute and inspect the Burst code’s values in the ordinary debugger
cards/4/explain: A Burst vs non-Burst difference is most often checks that were switched off, or the order of float operations. Cheap steps come first, the native debugger last.
cards/4/wrong/1: A struct’s ToString() does not work in Burst — it prints the type name. Log a literal or $"..." with primitives.
cards/4/wrong/2: It can be debugged: by turning compilation off, with Debug.Log, with a native debugger and Debug = true.
cards/4/wrong/3: With a managed debugger attached, Burst is turned off for that code path — you would see the managed version, which is exactly the one that works.
cards/5/q: A hot loop over a million elements has three movement rules, all known at compile time. Right now a FunctionPointer is called per element. What do you suggest?
cards/5/options/0: A generic MoveJob<TRule> with struct rules: Burst compiles a version per rule, the call can be inlined and the loop vectorized
cards/5/options/1: Keep the FunctionPointer: Burst inlines it like a normal call
cards/5/options/2: Put a Func<float, float, float> delegate in a job field
cards/5/options/3: Make the rules subclasses of a base class with a virtual method
cards/5/explain: If the type is known at compile time, you do not need an indirect call. The key is to schedule a concrete type (new MoveJob<Flee>), not through a generic method, or Burst will not find the version in a build.
cards/5/wrong/1: A call through a pointer is indirect — it cannot be inlined.
cards/5/wrong/2: A delegate is a managed object; Burst does not have them.
cards/5/wrong/3: A virtual call needs a class object — managed again.
cards/6/q: A trap. maxHits = 4, and sometimes objects the ray never hit take damage. Which line is to blame?
cards/6/explain: The first empty result is marked with collider == null, and the command does not overwrite the slots after it: hits from previous frames stay there. It needs break, not continue — the first empty result ends that command’s results.
cards/7/task: Replace the FunctionPointer in MoveJob with static polymorphism. Make the job generic: struct MoveJob<TRule> : IJobParallelFor where TRule : struct, ISpeedRule, with a field of type TRule; in Execute call rule.Speed(distance[i], baseSpeed). In Steering.Schedule, schedule new MoveJob<Flee> with Schedule(distance.Length, 64) and return the JobHandle. Do not make Schedule itself a generic method.
cards/7/checks/0/label: MoveJob is declared as MoveJob<T> : IJobParallelFor where T : struct, ISpeedRule
cards/7/checks/1/label: MoveJob has a field of the type parameter
cards/7/checks/4/label: A concrete type is scheduled: new MoveJob<Flee> … .Schedule(
cards/7/checks/5/label: Steering.Schedule is not a generic method
cards/7/explain: The rule type is known at compile time, so Burst builds MoveJob<Flee> separately, and the Speed call is an ordinary direct call that can be inlined. A concrete type at the scheduling site lets Burst find that version in a build too. Keep FunctionPointer for rules chosen at runtime.
cards/8/q: You moved the AI system into a Burst job. The Profiler shows the job at 0.1 ms, but the frame barely changed. What is most likely?
cards/8/options/0: The expensive part was not the computation but what surrounds it: gathering data from objects and scattering it back, or another part of the frame entirely — the hot spot had to be found with the profiler first
cards/8/options/1: Burst did not kick in, and without it the job does not run
cards/8/options/2: batchSize has to go down to 1
cards/8/options/3: The Profiler does not show the time of Burst jobs
cards/8/explain: Only what you sped up gets faster: if the computation was a small part of the frame, the frame barely moves. Markers and a measurement first, then move into Burst what is actually expensive.
cards/8/wrong/1: Without Burst the job still runs — as ordinary C#, only slower.
cards/8/wrong/2: batchSize changes how iterations are handed out; the job is already 0.1 ms.
cards/8/wrong/3: Burst jobs show up in the Timeline on worker threads like any other job.
cards/9/task: Replace 10 000 Spinner components with one SpinManager. In Awake, create a TransformAccessArray from items. Finish SpinJob: Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform) rotates localRotation by delta. In Update, compute delta on the main thread (Time.deltaTime only here), schedule new SpinJob { ... }.Schedule(transforms) and keep the JobHandle in a field. In LateUpdate call Complete(); in OnDestroy call Complete() and then transforms.Dispose().
cards/9/checks/1/label: Execute(int, TransformAccess) writes the transform’s rotation
cards/9/checks/2/label: The JobHandle is a field, and Update assigns it new SpinJob { ... }.Schedule(transforms)
cards/9/checks/5/label: OnDestroy calls Complete() first, then transforms.Dispose()
cards/9/explain: 10 000 Update calls become one Burst job on worker threads. Time is main-thread API, so the per-frame rotation is computed in Update and passed in a field. The objects sit at the scene root — otherwise the writing Schedule would hand them all to one thread. Without Complete() in OnDestroy, Dispose() could free the array under a running job.
cards/10/title: Practice in Unity: 10 000 cubes and a batch of rays
cards/10/body:
Setup (Unity 6, the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages, 40–60 minutes). A scene with a ground plane and a spawner that creates 10 000 cubes at the scene root; each has a Spinner component that rotates it in its own Update. Make a Development Build.

  1. Measure “before”. In the Profiler (CPU Usage, Timeline view), note the main-thread BehaviourUpdate time per frame.
  2. TransformAccessArray. Remove Spinner and hook up the SpinManager from the task above. In the Timeline, SpinJob should run on several worker threads, and the main thread should spend only the scheduling and Complete() on rotation.
  3. The hierarchy trap. Parent all the cubes under one object and measure again: the job drops to one thread. Move the cubes back to the root.
  4. A batch of rays. Add 500 agents and a GroundProbe with RaycastCommand; compare it with the Physics.Raycast version. The batch shows up as BatchQuery.ExecuteRaycastJob on worker threads. Wrap both versions in a ProfilerMarker.
  5. Burst Inspector. Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector: compare the MoveJob with a FunctionPointer and MoveJob<Flee>. The first has a call through an address in a register or memory inside the loop; the second has no call. Turn on Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed and see whether the multiplies are packed.

It worked if the main-thread rotation time dropped several times over, SpinJob is spread across worker threads, the one-root experiment showed the difference, the rays left the main thread, and you have written down the “before” and “after” numbers in milliseconds. Those numbers are what you tell in the interview: what you did, what you got, and why you stopped there.
